chapters.title: Chapter 3: Hedging a Mutual Fund or Diversified Portfolio with Nifty Options

lessons.title: Beta and Basis Risk: How Closely Your Portfolio Really Tracks the Nifty

children.text: Between late September 2024 and early March 2025, the Nifty 50 fell about 16%. Plenty of investors who watched that headline number were confused when they opened their CAS statement, because their portfolios had fallen a good deal more. Midcap and smallcap indices fell considerably harder than the Nifty. If those investors had been hedged with Nifty puts, their hedges would have paid out on the Nifty's fall, not theirs. The gap between the two has a name, basis risk, and the tool for measuring how big it is likely to be has another, beta. This lesson gives you both, with the spreadsheet formulas to calculate them yourself.

body.text: Beta tells you how much your portfolio tends to move when the Nifty moves. Correlation tells you how much you can trust that number. A Nifty hedge sized on beta protects the typical relationship, and basis risk is whatever happens outside it.

stats.label: Nifty 50
stats.context: September 2024 peak to early March 2025 low, approximate

children.text: Beta: How Much You Move When the Nifty Moves

markDefs.definition: A measure of how much a fund or portfolio tends to move for each 1% move in a benchmark index. A beta of 1.2 means it has typically moved about 1.2% for every 1% move in the index.

children.text: Beta

is the average sensitivity of your fund to the Nifty, measured from past returns. A Nifty 50 index fund has a beta very close to 1.0. A defensive large cap fund might sit around 0.85. A mid cap fund often runs above 1.0 against the Nifty 50. Beta is not a guarantee of how the next move will go. It is a summary of how the past ones went.

body.caption: R = periodic returns, ρ = correlation between them, σ = standard deviation of returns

children.text: The second form of the formula is the useful one to remember. Beta combines two separate things: how tightly the fund moves with the Nifty (correlation), and how big the fund's moves are compared with the Nifty's (the ratio of volatilities). Two funds can have the same beta for very different reasons, and that difference matters enormously for hedging.
Calculating Beta for Your Own Fund

Rohan from the previous lesson wants to check his flexi cap fund. He downloads 12 months of month-end NAVs from AMFI and month-end Nifty 50 closing levels from Nifty Indices, and converts both into monthly percentage returns.

body.caption: Monthly returns: Nifty 50 vs Rohan's flexi cap fund (illustrative data)

body.title: Monthly returns: Nifty 50 vs flexi cap fund

children.text: With the Nifty returns in column B and the fund returns in column C, three spreadsheet functions do all the work in Excel or Google Sheets:
Beta: =SLOPE(C2:C13, B2:B13)
returns 0.79. Note the order: the fund range comes first.
Correlation: =CORREL(B2:B13, C2:C13)
returns 0.94.
R-squared: =RSQ(C2:C13, B2:B13)
returns 0.89.

body.code:
import numpy as np

nifty = np.array([2.1, -1.8, 3.4, -4.2, 1.2, 0.6, -2.9, 4.8, -0.7, 1.9, -3.6, 2.5])
fund  = np.array([2.7, -2.5, 2.5, -3.4, 0.1, 1.7, -1.9, 3.8, -1.4, 2.3, -2.1, 1.3])

cov = np.cov(fund, nifty)          # 2x2 covariance matrix
beta = cov[0, 1] / cov[1, 1]       # Cov(fund, Nifty) / Var(Nifty)
corr = np.corrcoef(fund, nifty)[0, 1]

print(f"Beta: {beta:.2f}")          # Beta: 0.79
print(f"Correlation: {corr:.2f}")   # Correlation: 0.94
print(f"R-squared: {corr**2:.2f}")  # R-squared: 0.89
body.caption: The same calculation in Python, if you prefer code to spreadsheets

body.text: Twelve monthly returns is the bare minimum and gives a rough estimate. Two to three years of monthly data, or a year of weekly data, gives a steadier number. Whatever you use, calculate it against the Nifty 50 itself, since those are the options you will hedge with.

children.text: Correlation and R-squared: How Much to Trust the Beta

markDefs.definition: The share of a fund's return variation that is explained by the benchmark's movements, from 0 to 1. It equals the correlation squared.

children.text: Beta says how much the fund moves on average.
R-squared

says how much of the fund's behaviour that average actually explains. Rohan's flexi cap fund has an R-squared of 0.89: about 89% of its monthly ups and downs line up with the Nifty. The remaining 11% comes from its own stock picks, its mid and small cap holdings, and its cash. That 11% is the part a Nifty hedge cannot touch.

body.caption: A rough guide to reading R-squared for hedging purposes

cells: Strong relationship with meaningful fund-specific moves
Good, with some basis risk to allow for
Partly market-driven, partly its own story
Moderate. Expect noticeable gaps in both directions
Mostly driven by factors outside the Nifty
Low. The beta number is not a reliable basis for a hedge

body.title: Same beta, different hedge
body.question: Fund A has a beta of 0.8 against the Nifty 50 with an R-squared of 0.94. Fund B also has a beta of 0.8, but with an R-squared of 0.45. Which statement is correct?
options: Both funds can be hedged equally well, because their betas are the same.
Fund B is safer, because its low R-squared means it is less affected by the market.
A beta-sized Nifty hedge will be far more reliable for Fund A than for Fund B.
Fund A needs a larger hedge than Fund B.
body.explanation: Equal betas mean equal average sensitivity, so both would get the same size of hedge. But Fund B's low R-squared means most of its movement comes from outside the Nifty, so its actual losses in any given fall could be very different from what beta predicts. A low R-squared does not make a fund safer. It just means its risks are harder to hedge with the index.

children.text: Beta-Weighted Exposure: Turning a Portfolio Into Nifty Equivalents

Once you have a beta for each holding, you can express the whole portfolio as a single number: how many rupees of Nifty exposure it behaves like. Multiply each holding by its beta and add them up. This number, not the portfolio's market value, is what you hedge in the next lesson.

body.latex: \text{Beta-weighted exposure} = \sum_i V_i \times \beta_i \qquad \text{Portfolio beta} = \frac{\text{Beta-weighted exposure}}{\text{Total portfolio value}}
body.caption: V = value of each holding, β = its beta against the Nifty 50
Rohan's ₹25 lakh portfolio in Nifty-equivalent terms (betas vs Nifty 50, illustrative)

body.label: Rohan's portfolio beta
body.context: In an average month, his ₹25 lakh portfolio has behaved like ₹21.9 lakh of Nifty. Hedging the full ₹25 lakh would over-hedge the typical relationship.

body.title: Calculate beta-weighted exposure
body.prompt: Sunita holds ₹10 lakh in a Nifty 50 index fund (beta 1.0), ₹6 lakh in a mid cap fund (beta 1.2) and ₹4 lakh in a large cap fund (beta 0.9). What is her beta-weighted Nifty exposure, in rupees?
body.explanation: ₹10,00,000 × 1.0 + ₹6,00,000 × 1.2 + ₹4,00,000 × 0.9 = ₹10,00,000 + ₹7,20,000 + ₹3,60,000 = ₹20,80,000. Her ₹20 lakh portfolio behaves like ₹20.8 lakh of Nifty, a portfolio beta of 1.04, so a hedge sized on market value alone would slightly under-protect her.

children.text: Basis Risk: When the Fall Does Not Follow the Formula

markDefs.definition: The risk that a hedged position and its hedging instrument do not move as expected relative to each other, leaving part of a loss uncovered or over-covered.

children.text: Beta is an average, and crashes are not average months. In sharp sell-offs, mid and small caps often fall harder than their normal beta suggests, while funds with cash or foreign holdings may fall less. The difference between what beta predicted and what actually happened is
basis risk
. To see it clearly, imagine Rohan has a hedge that pays exactly his beta-weighted exposure times the Nifty's fall, with no strike gap and no premium. The Nifty then falls 15%.

body.caption: Nifty falls 15%: what beta predicted vs a plausible stress outcome (illustrative)

stats.label: Actual portfolio loss
stats.context: Mid and flexi cap funds fell harder than beta predicted

stats.label: Basis gap
stats.context: Loss left uncovered even by a perfectly sized hedge

body.text: Notice where the gap came from: the two holdings with the lowest R-squared among his Indian funds. The mid cap fund's normal beta of 1.15 became an effective 1.6 in this episode (24% ÷ 15%). This is typical of sharp sell-offs, when correlations rise and riskier holdings are sold hardest. If your portfolio leans towards mid and small caps, add a buffer to your hedge or accept that part of the loss will not be covered.

body.title: The R-squared link
body.textWithBlank: R-squared is equal to the correlation between the fund and the index, ___.
body.explanation: Rohan's flexi cap fund has a correlation of 0.94, and 0.94 × 0.94 ≈ 0.89, which is its R-squared.

body.title: The low-beta small cap fund
body.scenario: Vikas, 42, a dentist in Indore, holds ₹20 lakh in a single small cap fund. He calculates its beta against the Nifty 50 over two years and gets 0.75, with an R-squared of 0.48. "Great," he says. "My fund is less risky than the Nifty. I only need to hedge ₹15 lakh of Nifty exposure, and I'll be well protected."
body.prompt: What is wrong with Vikas's reasoning, and what should he take away from these numbers?
body.modelAnswer:
1. A beta below 1 does not mean lower risk here. Beta = correlation × (fund volatility ÷ Nifty volatility). With an R-squared of 0.48, the correlation is only about 0.69. For beta to be 0.75, the fund's volatility must be roughly 1.08 times the Nifty's, so it is actually more volatile, just less tied to it.
2. An R-squared of 0.48 means more than half of the fund's movement comes from outside the Nifty. A hedge sized on ₹15 lakh of Nifty exposure will be unreliable in both directions.
3. In sharp sell-offs, small caps have often fallen much harder than the Nifty, as they did in the 2024 to 2025 correction. His effective beta in a crash could be well above 1, leaving a large basis gap.
4. A Nifty hedge can still offset part of a broad market fall, but he should treat it as partial protection only, and consider a larger buffer.
5. The more important question is whether holding his entire equity allocation in one small cap fund suits his goals. Diversifying into large caps would both reduce his risk and make any future hedge far more effective.
The lesson: always read beta together with R-squared. A low beta with a low R-squared is a warning, not a comfort.

body.title: Measure your portfolio's real Nifty exposure
steps: Download at least 12 months, ideally 24 to 36, of month-end NAVs for each equity fund you hold from AMFI or your fund house.
Download month-end Nifty 50 closing levels for the same dates from Nifty Indices, and convert both into monthly returns.
Use SLOPE, CORREL and RSQ to calculate each fund's beta, correlation and R-squared against the Nifty 50.
Multiply each holding's value by its beta and add them to get your beta-weighted exposure and portfolio beta.
Mark any fund with an R-squared below 0.80 as a source of basis risk, and note how much of your portfolio it represents.

cards.definition: How much a fund tends to move for each 1% move in the benchmark: Cov(fund, index) ÷ Var(index).
How consistently two sets of returns move together, from −1 to +1.
Correlation squared. The share of a fund's movement explained by the index, and a guide to how reliable a beta-based hedge will be.
The sum of each holding's value × its beta. The Nifty-equivalent amount a portfolio behaves like.
The gap between a portfolio's actual loss and what the index hedge pays, usually largest for low R-squared holdings in sharp sell-offs.

points: Beta measures how much your fund tends to move when the Nifty moves. It equals correlation × the ratio of volatilities.
Calculate it yourself with SLOPE, CORREL and RSQ on at least 12 months of returns, against the Nifty 50 specifically.
R-squared tells you how much to trust beta. Above 0.9 is index-like; below 0.6, a beta-sized hedge is unreliable.
Beta-weighted exposure, the sum of value × beta across holdings, is the amount you actually hedge.
Basis risk is the gap between your real loss and the hedge payout. It grows in crashes, when mid and small caps fall harder than their beta suggests.
A low beta with a low R-squared is a warning sign, not a sign of safety.
